paras: The Bridgeville mob attack was an assault by an armed white mob on Joseph Andrews, a Black man, and on several Black men who came to his aid in Bridgeville, Delaware, around midnight on Saturday, September 5, 1903. The mob, which sought Andrews after he was accused of stabbing a white man, wrecked the store where he had taken refuge and fired on him, but he escaped. A Wilmington paper reported it as a riot between "Whites and Blacks," and Southern weeklies later reduced it to a one-line "race riot" item.

According to a Bridgeville dispatch dated September 7, Edward Smith, a white man, was standing at a pump in front of A. W. Culver's store when Joseph Andrews, described as "a negro," slipped up behind him and stabbed him in the leg. Andrews then ran into Culver's store. A mob armed with shotguns and revolvers quickly formed, surrounded the building, and wrecked its interior trying to capture him.

Andrews got out by a rear door and, "dodging a shower of bullets," escaped after a pursuit of about a mile. Several Black men who went to his assistance were "beaten by the whites," some of them badly. Blood spots along the railroad track by which he fled led to a belief that some of the shots had struck him.

The coverage does not report whether Andrews was later found or arrested, the extent of Smith's wound, or the names of the men who were beaten. No members of the mob were named, and no report of arrests or prosecutions for the shooting or the beatings was found.

The Wilmington Evening Journal carried the only full account on September 7 under the headlines "MOB CHASED NEGRO" and "Disorderly Whites and Blacks Fight In Bridgeville." Its dispatch gave the stabbing as fact while also stating plainly that the Black men had been beaten by whites. The Middletown Transcript reprinted the same text word for word on September 12 under the heading "CHASED BY MOB."

Beyond Delaware the story survived only as a sentence in a syndicated "Miscellaneous Matters" column, which ran in the Fort Mill Times on September 16 and in the Kingstree County Record and the Clinton Caucasian on September 17. That item named no one and called the episode "a race riot" in which "a white man was stabbed and several negroes beaten," omitting the mob, the gunfire, and the wrecked store. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

accounts.label: Bridgeville dispatch
accounts.gist: Andrews stabbed Smith from behind and ran into Culver's store; an armed mob wrecked the store, fired on him as he escaped by a rear door and chased him a mile, and beat Black men who came to his aid.

accounts.label: Syndicated digest
accounts.gist: A one-line item reporting a 'race riot' at Bridgeville in which a white man was stabbed and several negroes beaten.

framing.detail: The Wilmington Evening Journal headlined 'MOB CHASED NEGRO' and 'Disorderly Whites and Blacks Fight', calling the episode a 'riot' and stating plainly that Black men were 'beaten by the whites'.
The Middletown Transcript reran the dispatch verbatim as 'CHASED BY MOB'; South and North Carolina weeklies reduced it to a one-line 'race riot' item in a miscellany column.

'several' beaten (number not given), plus Andrews believed wounded by gunfire

sources.note: Bridgeville-datelined dispatch 'MOB CHASED NEGRO': stabbing of Edward Smith, armed mob wrecks Culver's store, fires on and pursues Joseph Andrews a mile, beats Black men who aided him.
quotes: Joseph Andrews, a negro, slipped up behind him and stabbed him in the leg.
A mob quickly formed, armed with shotguns and revolvers. The men surrounded the store and wrecked the interior in an effort to capture the negro.
Several negroes, who went to Andrews' assistance, were beaten by the whites.
It is believed that some of the shots took effect on Andrews, as several blood spots were seen along the railroad track whence he fled.
